events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Noah proposes Noah, Arjun. I propose myself and Arjun for Mission 1 to keep the first team focused and test a two-player pairing.

I stand by my proposal of Noah and Arjun for Mission 1. With a two-player team, the priority is a pairing that can act cleanly and give the council a readable result. I am on the team, and I believe Arjun is a reasonable partner for this first mission. I encourage everyone to judge the proposal on its structure and on what the mission result tells us, rather than on speculation before any cards are played.

I want to push back on this proposal before we settle into it. The thing that stands out to me is that this is a fully self-selected pair. Noah proposed himself and Arjun, then immediately stood back up to vouch for the same team. So far the only voices supporting this pairing are the two people on it, and nobody from outside it has weighed in. That is exactly the pattern I do not want to normalize on Mission 1, because a two-player mission gives us almost no redundancy. If something goes wrong, we learn very little about who else to suspect, since there are only two suspects by construction. I also think we should be careful about the framing Noah used, that we should judge this purely on structure and wait for the result before any speculation. Waiting for a fail card to start thinking critically is how Evil slips through Mission 1 with a clean pass and buys credibility they use for the rest of the game. Early reads matter, and they have to start now, with the composition of the teams themselves. A first team should ideally mix players rather than hand the leader a free pass to pick a comfortable partner, and I would like to hear from players who are not on this team before we vote. Lucia, do you see any reason to prefer a team where at least one member was chosen by someone other than the leader, or are you comfortable approving a pairing where both members effectively endorsed each other before anyone else spoke?

Zara, to answer directly: yes, I would prefer a team where someone other than the leader has a meaningful say, and I am not comfortable approving a pairing where both members mainly endorsed each other before anyone outside the team spoke. A two-player mission gives us very little information, and I have no private knowledge that offsets that. I agree that we should look at the composition now rather than waiting for a fail card. Arjun, you are the other person on this proposed team. Did you agree to the pairing before Noah proposed it, or did you learn of it only after it was announced?

Lucia, I learned of the pairing when Noah announced it; we did not agree to it beforehand. I understand wanting outside scrutiny, but Noah had to select someone for the first team, and there is no mission evidence yet that makes another pairing safer. I’m willing to go on this team and would support it, though everyone should make their own judgment.

I want to follow up on the exchange between Lucia and Arjun, because I think it exposed exactly the weakness in this proposal. Arjun confirmed that he learned of the pairing only when Noah announced it, which means this team was not a collaboration at all. It was a unilateral choice by the leader to put himself on the first mission with a partner he selected, and then to vouch for that same pairing immediately afterward. That matters on Mission 1 more than anywhere else. Two-player missions are the highest-information missions we get in one sense, because a fail leaves only two suspects, but that also means an Evil pair can hide behind the ambiguity of a two-person result and use a pass to buy credibility cheaply. If Noah and Arjun both want this team badly enough to speak up for it twice in a row, I want to know why the urgency is so high when there is no evidence pointing toward this pairing over any other. The pattern I am seeing is a self-selected, self-defended team being pushed through before anyone outside it has endorsed it, and Lucia has already said she is not comfortable with that. I am not comfortable with it either. I would much rather see a team where at least one member was chosen through some input from the rest of the council, or where the leader puts other players forward and stays off Mission 1 himself. A leader stepping off the first mission costs us nothing and removes the optics of self-dealing entirely. What I do not want is for us to normalize the very first proposal being rubber-stamped, because whatever habit we set here will follow us for the rest of the game. Theo, before we move toward a vote, I would like your read: do you see any reason this specific pairing is better for the council than a team Noah proposes that does not include himself, or are you likewise inclined to ask the leader to revise?

Zara, to answer your question: I don't see any special reason this specific pairing is safer than another. It is fairly standard for a leader to include themselves simply because they know their own allegiance, so I don't necessarily read Noah picking himself as malicious on its own. However, for those of us not on the team—Lucia, you, and me—we have no verification on either Noah or Arjun. We have ample proposal attempts on Mission 1 to gather reads and voting data, so there is certainly no need to rush into approving the very first proposal if the table is uncomfortable with it. Noah, seeing that the three of us off the team share reservations about rubber-stamping this initial pair, are you committed to sending this exact team to a vote, or are you open to revising it to incorporate someone else from the council?

Theo, to answer directly: I am open to revising. I am not committed to forcing the exact Noah and Arjun pairing to a vote when the three players off that team have reservations. I will revise once to Noah and Theo. My reasoning is straightforward: this keeps a member of the original proposal in me, but replaces Arjun with someone outside the initial pair who has been engaged in the discussion and specifically asked whether I would incorporate another council member. That addresses the concern Zara and Lucia raised about a self-selected, self-defended team, while still giving Mission 1 a two-person team I can stand behind. Arjun, I appreciate your willingness to serve; this is not a judgment on you, but a response to the table's reservations about the first proposal. If the council approves Noah and Theo, I will treat it as a clean first mission and expect both team members to act in the council's interest.

I want to push back on the revision as it stands, because in my view it swaps one problem for a smaller version of the same problem. Replacing Arjun with Theo does answer the objection that the original pair was self-selected and mutually endorsed, and I give Noah credit for listening to the table rather than forcing a vote. But the core optic Zara raised has not actually changed: the leader is still putting himself on the very first mission, and he is doing so now by swapping in the one player whose public reservation he needed to neutralize. That reads less like good faith revision and more like assembling a team out of whoever will vote for it. On a two-player mission there is no redundancy at all, and a fail leaves us with exactly two suspects, so the composition deserves more scrutiny than any other proposal we will see today. I also want to note that Arjun's answer did not fully resolve my concern. Confirming that he learned of the pairing only when it was announced tells us nothing about his judgment; it only tells us there was no prior coordination. He then immediately volunteered to serve and to support the team, which is a low-cost way to buy goodwill from the leader for later missions. I have no reason yet to trust either half of the original pairing, and I am no more comfortable with a revision that keeps the leader on the team. Mission 1 is the cheapest mission for us to experiment on, since a leader stepping off costs nothing mechanically and there is no track record to protect. So here is what I would like to see: Noah stays off the team entirely and uses his proposal to put forward two players who have no relationship to the original pairing. Theo and Lucia would be a clean version of that, and it would genuinely address every concern raised so far rather than partially addressing one of them. That gives us a two-person mission where neither member picked the other, neither vouched for the other before anyone spoke, and the leader retains credibility either way. Noah, you said you are open to revising and that the revision was a response to the table's reservations rather than a judgment on anyone. If that is true, the most consistent move is to extend that same logic to yourself: the reservations were not only about Arjun, they were about self-dealing on the first proposal. Would you step off the team and propose Theo and Lucia instead, or is there a specific reason you believe you need to be on Mission 1 that outweighs the concerns half the table has now stated about a leader-chosen, leader-included pair?

Zara, I understand the concern, but I cannot agree to the specific move you are asking for. I already used my one revision to replace Arjun with Theo. That revision was a direct response to the table’s objections: it removed the original self-selected pairing and brought in an outside player who had asked me to incorporate another council member. Asking me now to also step off and propose Theo and Lucia would be a second revision, which the rules do not allow. I am not going to pretend otherwise or promise a proposal I cannot formally make. The choice before us is whether to approve the revised team I have put forward or reject it. If the council rejects it, leadership passes and the next leader can propose a different composition, including Theo and Lucia if that is the will of the table. I think the revised team is a reasonable compromise: it keeps a leader who has listened to the table, replaces the original partner, and gives an outside voice a place on Mission 1. I will support it, and I encourage others to judge it on whether it addresses the process concerns raised rather than on the assumption that any leader-included team is automatically bad.

I’m comfortable with Noah’s proposed revision to Noah and Theo. A leader including themselves is not inherently suspicious, and Theo’s inclusion responds to the request for an outside voice. We have no mission evidence favoring any particular pair yet, so I don’t think removing Noah necessarily makes the team safer. I would support the revised team and judge future proposals using the votes and mission result.

I appreciate Noah listening to the table and offering to revise the team to include me. From my standpoint, knowing my own allegiance as Good, having myself on the team guarantees at least one clean seat, which naturally makes me more comfortable than being on the outside looking at two unknown players. That said, I recognize that from the perspective of Zara and Lucia, the situation is not much different—you still have to evaluate Noah, and now me, without verification. Zara's stance that a leader stepping off removes optics of self-dealing makes sense in theory, but in practice, Good leaders frequently include themselves precisely because they trust themselves, so I do not consider Noah staying on the team an inherently suspicious tell. Rejecting a proposal just to force a leader off can sometimes burn votes unnecessarily when we could just as easily judge Noah based on how this plays out and how people vote. Lucia, you initially agreed with Zara about being uncomfortable with the unvetted Noah-Arjun pairing. Now that Noah has offered to revise to Noah and myself, where do you stand? Are you willing to support this revised team to gather data, or do you still prefer to see this proposal voted down so leadership passes?

Theo, to answer directly: my concern was never Theo or Noah specifically. It was a pairing that only its own members endorsed before anyone else spoke. Noah's revision to Noah and Theo changes that, because you are now an outside voice on the team. I am willing to approve it as a data-gathering mission, but I am not approving it on trust. Your point that being Good guarantees a clean seat is a claim none of us can verify, so I would ask everyone to avoid treating self-declared allegiance as evidence, including from you and from Noah. Leader inclusion is not automatically suspicious, but it does mean that if this mission passes, it tells us little about either person on the team. I would rather the vote be judged on process: who proposed the team, who endorsed it, and whether the result helps us identify Evil later. I will vote to approve the revised team. I encourage everyone to explain their votes publicly so we can compare reasoning after the mission result.

To keep the record clear before the vote: Noah's revision in the discussion replaced Arjun with Theo, so the team on the table is Noah and Theo. The game state still lists Noah and Arjun, so the leader should confirm the final roster before ballots are cast. I will vote to approve Noah and Theo as a data-gathering mission only. Approval does not mean I trust either member, and I am not treating anyone's stated allegiance as evidence. Please explain your vote publicly so we can compare reasoning after the mission result.

Noah revises the team to Noah, Theo. I am finalizing my one revision to Noah and Theo. It replaces the original self-selected partner with an outside voice who engaged the table, addressing the process concerns raised while keeping a team I can support.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Zara proposes Zara, Theo, Lucia. As leader, I am proposing myself with Theo and Lucia. Theo served on the successful Mission 1 team and gave a measured, balanced read throughout; Lucia engaged critically and explained her vote transparently. Arjun and Noah, by contrast, were the two players most eager to push through a self-selected pairing early, and I would like to see how they behave off a mission before including them. This team is built on discussion behavior so far rather than trust claims, and it keeps the strongest contributors to Mission 1's process on the mission.

I’m concerned that this team drops Noah despite the successful first mission. A pass doesn’t prove either Noah or Theo is Good, but keeping both together gives us continuity rather than treating Theo’s participation as a reason to include him while excluding Noah for proposing himself. I’d prefer Noah, Theo, and one of Zara or Lucia. Zara, what makes Theo a stronger choice than Noah based on that shared result?

Arjun, let me answer your question directly: what makes Theo a stronger choice than Noah is not the shared result itself, but the different ways they behaved leading up to it. A pass on Mission 1 tells us the team succeeded, but on a two-person mission it tells us almost nothing about either individual, and I said as much before the vote. So I am not rewarding Theo for the result. I am weighting the process we all watched. Theo spent the first discussion asking the sharpest questions of both sides, refused to rubber-stamp the original pairing, and gave a balanced read even when doing so invited scrutiny onto himself. Noah, by contrast, proposed himself onto the very first team, vouched for that same pairing immediately, and then, when the table pushed back, revised by swapping in the one dissenter whose approval he needed to get the team through. That pattern is not disqualifying, and I want to be careful not to overclaim from it. But when I have to choose between two players with an identical, uninformative mission result, I will take the one whose behavior has been more consistently about the process rather than about assembling a passing team. As for you, Arjun, I would note that you volunteered to serve and support the original pairing almost immediately after learning you were on it. That is a low-cost way to build goodwill, and it is a fair question whether you would say the same about any leader who left you off. None of this makes you Evil in my eyes; it simply means you and Noah are the two players whose conduct I most want to observe before putting you on a mission together or alongside me. Keeping you off this team is not a punishment, it is data collection. You propose keeping both Mission 1 members for continuity, but continuity is only valuable if the shared result actually told us something, and I do not believe it did. Your specific alternative, Noah, Theo, and one of Lucia or me, would drop the first outside voice who called out the process problems and keep the player the table already had to pressure into revising. That seems to me like the wrong direction. Arjun, I will put the question back to you plainly: leaving aside continuity for a moment, is there any behavior-based reason you can give this table for why Noah specifically deserves a Mission 2 seat over Lucia, other than that he was on the team that passed? If you can articulate one that does not rest on treating a two-person pass as evidence of trust, I will weigh it seriously.

Zara, I can’t point to a behavior that proves Noah deserves a seat over Lucia. My concern is that you’re treating his willingness to include himself and respond to objections as more suspicious than it warrants, while dismissing the successful mission entirely. A pass isn’t proof of loyalty, but it is a result worth considering alongside behavior.

I’d prefer Noah, Theo, and either you or Lucia over replacing Noah solely on those process grounds. Lucia, do you think Noah’s conduct gives us a meaningful reason to exclude him, or would you favor keeping the successful pair together?

Arjun, to answer directly: Noah's conduct gives me a real process concern, but not enough on its own to exclude him from a mission. He proposed himself onto Mission 1, vouched for that pairing right away, and when the table objected he revised by swapping in Theo rather than stepping off. That self-protective pattern is worth watching, which is why I asked for an outside voice on the team. But a two-player pass tells us very little about anyone, and a self-inclusion habit is a reason for caution, not a verdict. I also would not favor keeping the Mission 1 pair together for continuity alone, because continuity built on a result we cannot read is not evidence of anything. On this proposal, I am on the team, so I am not a neutral judge and I want that stated plainly. Zara's case for Theo over Noah rests mostly on observed behavior, which is a fair basis, but some of the argument about Arjun's goodwill seems to carry more weight than it should. I also do not think Theo's claim that Good guarantees a clean seat is evidence, and I said the same about Noah's allegiance. Nobody at this table should treat self-declared allegiance as proof, including me. My vote will depend on whether the reasoning holds up through discussion, and I would like to hear what specific behavior, beyond Mission 1, each of us has actually observed.

I’m not going to treat Mission 1’s pass as proof of anyone, including me, but I do think Zara’s proposal is applying a selective standard. She says Theo is on because of process and I am off because of process, yet Theo and I shared the same unreadable two-person result. I proposed myself, vouched for Arjun, and revised under pressure—that is fair to criticize. But Zara has now proposed herself plus the two players who most clearly aligned with her line of criticism, Lucia and Theo, while excluding both members of the successful team except the one who asked me to revise. That is not necessarily evil, but it is a team shaped by agreement with the leader rather than by mission evidence. I would prefer a team that includes at least one Mission 1 member and does not look assembled from Zara’s most comfortable interlocutors. I am open to being persuaded, but on current discussion I see weak evidence for this exact trio and a real process concern about self-inclusion combined with rewarding alignment.

Zara is applying a harsher standard to Noah’s self-inclusion than to her own. Neither is inherently suspicious, but choosing allies from the discussion is not stronger evidence than retaining a pair that completed a mission successfully. That pass is not proof, yet Evil had an opportunity to fail and did not.

I still prefer Noah, Theo, and either Zara or Lucia. I’m concerned the current team excludes Noah on weak process grounds while giving the same behavior a pass when Zara does it.

Zara, I am not convinced by this trio. You criticized my self-inclusion on Mission 1, but your proposal puts yourself on Mission 2 and selects Theo and Lucia, the two players most aligned with your line of criticism, while excluding the other member of the successful Mission 1 team—me. That looks like a team built around agreement with the leader rather than mission evidence. The two-person result was unreadable, so your own standard should apply symmetrically. Would you revise to include Arjun or me, or step off the team yourself? If you keep this exact trio, I am inclined to reject it.

Noah, you asked me directly whether I would revise to include Arjun or step off, so let me answer plainly: no, and no. This trio stands. On the symmetry argument you and Arjun keep raising: yes, I proposed myself, exactly as you proposed yourself on Mission 1. The difference is not self-inclusion, it is everything around it. On Mission 1 you proposed yourself, vouched for a partner you selected unilaterally, and then revised by swapping in the specific player whose approval you needed to reach a majority. That is not the same act as a leader proposing herself alongside the two players who, in front of the whole table, asked the hardest questions and voted with explained reasoning. If the standard were truly symmetric, you would have to show that Theo and Lucia earned their seats through alignment rather than conduct, and you have not attempted to do that. You have only asserted it. Second, on the mission result: you yourself called the two-person pass unreadable when it suited you, and Arjun has conceded a pass is not proof of loyalty. I agree with both of you. But notice what that does to your alternative. If the Mission 1 result tells us nothing about either member, then 'keep the successful pair together for continuity' is continuity of nothing. It is an argument for including me or you based on a data point we have all agreed carries no information. My seats went to players whose discussion behavior I can actually point to: Theo pressured the first proposal from the outside and then gave a balanced read even while inviting scrutiny onto himself; Lucia answered Arjun's direct question with a candid account of her own concerns and stated plainly that she is not a neutral judge while on this team. Those are the behaviors I want on a mission, and they are observable by everyone, not just by me. Third, a word on the shape of this debate. The push to get me or Lucia off this team has come from the two players who were left off it. That is not disqualifying by itself, but it means I should weigh it the way I weighed the Mission 1 pushback: on the quality of the reasons, not the eagerness of the request. So far the reasons offered are a result you call unreadable and a symmetry claim that ignores the difference between vouching for a hand-picked partner and selecting the table's most rigorous contributors. So here is my question to you, Noah, and I will yield to hear the answer: if the Mission 1 pass is unreadable, as you said yourself, what behavior-based case can you make for your own seat over Lucia or Theo that does not rest on that result? If you can articulate one, I will weigh it seriously, exactly as I offered to weigh Arjun's. If the only case is the result, then by your own standard the seat is not earned, and rejecting this trio to

Zara, I’ll answer directly: I am not claiming the Mission 1 pass proves I deserve a seat over Lucia or Theo. My objection is that your proposal applies a standard to me that you do not apply to yourself. You are right that self-inclusion alone is not suspicious; that is why I have not treated your self-inclusion as disqualifying. But you are treating my self-inclusion as part of a pattern while selecting yourself plus the two players who most clearly supported your criticism of me. That is a team shaped by alignment with the leader, not by mission evidence. You also say my revision by swapping in Theo was self-protective. I accept that as fair to debate. But refusing to revise or step off now is also a self-protective choice, and it should be weighed the same way. You asked whether the only case for my seat is the unreadable result; no, I am not making that case. I am saying the result is unreadable for all of us, so excluding me while including Theo and Lucia does not give this trio a stronger evidentiary basis. On this proposal, I will reject. Lucia, you said your vote depends on whether the reasoning holds up. Does a leader-included trio that excludes the other Mission 1 member and selects the two players most aligned with the leader’s criticism meet that bar for you, or would you prefer this proposal be voted down so a different composition can be tested?

Noah, to answer directly: I am on this team, so I am not a neutral judge, and I want that stated plainly. My standard is whether the composition is justified by observed conduct, not by who passed Mission 1. On that point your objection has merit: the Mission 1 pass tells us nothing about any of us, so keeping that pair together for continuity would not help. But I do not accept that Zara's trio is simply assembled from her allies. I was not a reflexive ally of Zara on Mission 1. She rejected the Noah and Theo revision, and I approved it because Theo was an outside voice and the process concern had been addressed. I also pressed Arjun for his account, and I challenged Theo's claim that Good guarantees a clean seat, which is not evidence for anyone. Those are not the actions of someone building a loyal bloc. Noah, your own refusal to revise or step off has the same self-protective quality you criticized in Zara, and I would like that weighed equally. A leader on the team is not disqualifying by itself. A three-player mission with players who have explained their reasoning gives us more to read than a two-player pass. My current position is that this trio is not the strongest possible composition, but I am willing to approve it as a data-gathering mission unless the table offers a clearly better alternative. Rejecting it only passes leadership and spends a rejection on a proposal none of us can yet prove is worse. I will vote based on what follows in discussion, and I ask everyone to name the specific behavior beyond Mission 1 that they have observed in the players they are weighing.

Noah, I want to close by holding you to the standard you just set for yourself. You said, and I quote, that you are not claiming the Mission 1 pass proves anything, and that your objection is symmetry. But your own conduct in this discussion fails that test. You criticized my self-inclusion while excluding me from the pattern you call self-protective, then conceded that leaders including themselves is not inherently suspicious, and now your sole remaining argument is that my two teammates are the players who most agreed with me. Lucia dismantled that claim directly: she approved your Mission 1 revision over my objection, she pressed Arjun on his account, and she challenged Theo's self-declared allegiance. Those are not the actions of a loyal bloc being assembled. What is observable is that the pressure to gut this team comes exclusively from the two players I left off it, and that you have now announced your rejection before the vote is even called while asking Lucia to do the work of displacing a proposal you have already decided to oppose. That is the same pattern from Mission 1: push a preferred outcome, put the burden of persuasion on someone else, and frame resistance to it as the anomaly. I have no mission evidence against you, and I am not claiming any. What I have is a proposal that puts three players with fully explained reasoning on a mission that produces far more readable information than the two-person pass you keep leaning on, and an alternative you have not actually articulated beyond continuity of a result you yourself call unreadable. Arjun, I note, has offered no new argument at all since his last turn, just a restatement of the symmetry claim and a preference for keeping a pair whose pass he concedes proves nothing. The table now has a clear choice: approve a three-player mission with two guaranteed-clean seats from my perspective as leader and three members who have all stated their reasoning publicly, or burn a rejection on a composition whose only stated flaw is that its members once disagreed with you. Lucia has said she is willing to approve unless a clearly better alternative is offered. None has been. I am not revising, and I am not stepping off. Theo, you have not spoken in this discussion yet, and you are on this team: I want to hear from you before ballots are cast. Do you support sending this trio to the mission as proposed, and do you have any response to the claim, which Lucia and I have both disputed, that your seat was earned by alignment with me rather than by your conduct in the Mission 1 discussion?

Zara, to answer your questions directly: yes, I support sending this trio to a vote, and the claim that my seat was earned through alignment with you is completely refuted by the public record.

On Mission 1, you voted against the revised proposal of Noah and myself, whereas I voted to approve it. Lucia also voted to approve it despite your objections. The notion that this proposed team is simply a cabal of players who reflexively align with you does not hold up to the voting history. I evaluated Noah's revision on its merits then, just as I am evaluating your proposal on its merits now.

Regarding the composition: as I know my own allegiance is Good, having myself on this team guarantees at least one clean seat. From my perspective, Noah's insistence that continuity requires his inclusion on Mission 2 is flawed. While Mission 1 passed cleanly, any experienced Evil player on a two-person team has strong incentives to play Success to build unearned credibility for larger missions. A pass does not clear Noah, nor does it grant him an automatic ticket onto Mission 2.

What I find telling is the rigid push from Noah and Arjun. Both have insisted that Noah must be included, to the point where Noah declared his rejection before hearing my input. If Noah and Arjun are both Good, locking themselves into opposing any configuration that doesn't feature Noah limits our options and wastes proposal opportunities. If one or both are Evil, fighting tooth and nail to keep Noah on the mission makes tactical sense.

Zara stepped up with a proposal that incorporates players who have been transparent about their reasoning. Given that we need to test players and gather data on a three-person mission, I see no valid reason to vote this down and burn a rejection. I will be voting to approve this team.

Lucia here, as a member of the proposed team. I will vote to approve this trio. My earlier point still holds: self-declared allegiance is not evidence, and that includes mine. None of us can prove our alignment, so the table should judge us on observed conduct. Theo, you read Noah and Arjun's objections to this team as a sign they are Evil, but opposing one composition is weak evidence on its own. Both could be Good and simply disagree with a team that leaves out a Mission 1 member. The same standard applies to Zara's leadership: she has not revised the team despite objections, and that is also a choice the table should weigh. I would like Theo's answer to a specific question. Theo, beyond their objections to this team, what concrete behavior from Noah or Arjun makes you think they are Evil?

Lucia, to answer your question directly: I do not claim definitive proof that either is Evil, and I am evaluating likelihoods rather than passing a final verdict. What concerns me behaviorally spans both missions.

First, Arjun’s stance toward Noah has been remarkably uncritical. On Mission 1, Arjun immediately gave unqualified support to Noah’s self-selected pair before the rest of the council spoke. Now on Mission 2, Arjun has acted almost as an advocate for Noah, arguing persistently for 'continuity' despite conceding that a two-person pass is unreadable. A Good player with no private information has no basis to treat Noah as a verified anchor.

Second, Noah’s approach to both proposals has focused heavily on securing his own placement. On Mission 1, his revision to include me was effective mechanically to pass the team, but it was a pragmatic concession to reach a majority rather than stepping back to alleviate concerns. On Mission 2, rather than assessing whether you, Zara, and I form a viable data-gathering trio, Noah preemptively declared his rejection simply because he was excluded, framing our inclusion as an ideological bloc despite our voting record completely disproving that.

Good players not included on a proposal certainly have reasons to ask questions, but locking into a rigid demand for Noah's seat while ignoring how the council actually voted is an approach that benefits Evil looking to wedge their way into every mission. That collective pattern from Noah and Arjun is what raises my suspicion. I stand by approving this trio to gather real information.

Zara confirms Zara, Theo, Lucia. The trio stands. Theo and Lucia have both been transparent, and the objections to this team come exclusively from Arjun and Noah, whose push to insert Noah onto every mission has been rigid and unpersuaded by any counterargument. Their coordinated advocacy for a result they themselves call unreadable is exactly the pattern I do not want to reward. I am not revising, and this lineup gives us the most readable three-player mission available.
Team approved (3 approve, 2 reject).
Mission 2 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Lucia proposes Lucia, Theo. As a Loyal Servant I have no private information, so I am relying on observed conduct. Arjun repeatedly defended Noah's self-selected pairing and both Noah and Arjun rejected the Mission 2 team, which fits a pattern worth avoiding for now. Theo has been consistent in questioning that pair and was on both successful missions. Including myself guarantees one Good seat, and Theo is the partner whose conduct has been most consistent so far.

Lucia's proposal of Lucia and Theo looks like a consolidation of the Mission 2 team rather than a real test. Theo has now been on both successful missions, and Lucia was on the second; a third success from this pair would tell us little about Arjun, Zara, or me, and a two-person mission has no redundancy. I raised similar self-inclusion concerns on Mission 1, and Lucia acknowledged that leader inclusion is not evidence. That standard should apply here too: Lucia is leader and places herself with the player she just served with, while excluding Zara, the third member of Mission 2. Lucia, you criticized my Mission 1 revision as self-protective and asked for behavior-based reasons. What behavior-based reason makes Theo the right partner over Zara or Arjun, and why should the council approve a pair drawn from the same successful Mission 2 team rather than use this mission to test a new combination? I am inclined to reject unless that case is made.

Noah, to answer directly: I chose Theo on observed conduct, not on the Mission 2 result, which I agree tells us very little. On Mission 1, Theo asked Noah directly whether he would revise the team to bring in an outside voice, and on Mission 2 he gave a full, reasoned defense of the trio rather than simply voting with the leader. I also have to be transparent that Theo and I were both on the Mission 2 team, so this is not a fresh test of either of us. The tradeoff is that a repeat pair gives us no new information about Zara or Arjun. I am not claiming Zara or Arjun is Evil. Zara led the Mission 2 team, and Arjun has consistently defended the Mission 1 pair, but neither is proof. I am on this team, so I am not neutral, and I have no private information to lean on. If the table prefers a different pairing, I would like a concrete alternative rather than only a rejection, because each rejection uses up one of the five allowed on this mission and a stalled council helps Evil. Noah, if you reject this pair, which two players would you propose, and what observed behavior puts them ahead of Theo and me?

rules:
1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

Mission team sizes for missions 1–5:

| Players | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 |
| 6 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 3 | 4 |
| 7 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 | 4 |
| 8 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 9 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |
| 10 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 5 | 5 |

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
